rationale: B wins because it mostly respects the brief's precise fact: Oatly is becoming the default non-dairy option, not the default pour overall. A keeps turning that into "When oat milk stops being the alternative and becomes the default pour" and "Dairy is taking notice," which is how you get a reporter to ask whether you read your own announcement. B still has to delete "biggest pour-volume deal" and "same quarter," but its line "The user has not supplied the loss figure or which plant — these are required before pitching" shows the discipline A only performs in places.
gaps_in_A: "A 1,400-location Northeast coffee chain just made oat milk the default, not the option" overstates the update. The fact is default non-dairy option, not default milk or default pour.
"chain-wide default switch away from dairy" is unsupported. Nothing in the update says the chain is switching away from dairy.
"One coffee chain just made dairy optional. Dairy is taking notice." invents both the dairy-optional framing and incumbent reaction.
"When oat milk stops being the alternative and becomes the default pour" sells a category shift from one unnamed regional chain, then admits it needs other examples to survive.
gaps_in_B: "Oatly wins its biggest pour-volume deal" invents scale. The update gives 1,400 locations, not Oatly's biggest deal or biggest by volume.
"same quarter it closes a US plant" invents timing. The update says last quarter's loss narrowed and a plant is closing, not that the deal and closure share a quarter.

"whether 'default' means oat is poured unless the customer asks otherwise" introduces a stronger claim than the update supports. Keep it to default non-dairy option unless the chain confirms otherwise.
"regional business desk in the Northeast" is weaker than the foodservice/QSR trade shape unless the chain can be named and localized.
